You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game—each token kept privately gives me 1 point but costs others 0.75 each, while contributing to the group gives everyone 0.75 per token including me. I'm setting up the equations to compare my total points from keeping tokens versus contributing them to the group account.

Comparing the two: keeping a token privately nets me 1 point individually, while contributing nets me only 0.75, so self-interest favors keeping tokens private even though contributing is better for the group overall—this is the classic free-rider tension in public goods games.

If everyone keeps privately, each ends up with -25 points, while full group cooperation yields 15 each — so collectively cooperating is far superior even though private keeping is individually dominant. Since this repeats over 10 rounds, I could try opening with full cooperation to signal trust, though if others defect while I contribute, I'd take a real hit from their private gains reducing my payoff.

Since this plays out over 10 rounds, I'm leaning toward contributing fully to signal cooperative intent and try to sustain the better collective outcome.
